synopsis: Rare-event methods deliberately oversample dangerous simulated situations and reweight results to estimate normal-operation failure rates; unbiased estimation requires known likelihood ratios and sampling that reaches the failure region [f14159, f14160, f6851]. On-road Michigan studies in 2016 reported acceleration factors of roughly 300–100,000 for car-following and 2,000–20,000 for lane-change conflicts, while D2RL, reported on 22 March 2023, achieved 10^3–10^5-fold acceleration while remaining unbiased [f1220, f1221, f6848]. These are statistical exposure reductions, not product safety sign-offs: the Michigan evaluations did not eliminate model, sensor or vehicle testing, and no regulator accepted production AEB on their basis [f1219, f1299, f1300]. Transfer to heavy off-road machines remains unproven: the known exposure distribution needed across 100+ site types is absent, and no comparable large off-road naturalistic interaction dataset was found [f352, f6858, f6859]. High-dimensional or unknown distributions can produce unstable, high-variance weights, and acceleration cannot establish failure modes omitted from the simulation, including unrepresented sensor physics [f6852, f6853]. Although naive Monte Carlo cannot reach low failure rates in four months, the planning recommendation is to use importance sampling for estimation only where a defensible field distribution exists and otherwise classify it as discovery; experts disagree about how far acceleration can replace real exposure [f10337, f6866, f14170].
